Subscription-Free Living: Using Global Dividend Giants to Pay for Your Daily Tech Habits
article:
Netflix
(NASDAQ: NFLX) on the weekend,
Spotify
(NYSE: SPOT) on the commute, and an AI tool that drafts your emails.
Each subscription feels cheap on its own.
Add them up though, and you could be spending hundreds of dollars a year without noticing.
So what if your salary didn’t have to foot the bill?
That’s the idea behind subscription-free living: building a portfolio of global dividend payers whose payouts quietly cover your digital habits.
Here’s how much you’d need, which companies to look at, and how to set it up.
How Much Are Your Digital Subscriptions Really Costing You?
Subscription
Illustrative Monthly Cost (S$)
Video streaming (e.g. Netflix)
20
Music streaming (e.g. Spotify)
12
Cloud storage (e.g. iCloud)
4
AI productivity tools
30
Other digital services
14
Total
80
That S$80 a month works out to S$960 a year.
That’s S$4,800 over five years, and S$9,600 over 10 years before any price increases.
So what would it take to cover S$960 a year with dividends?
Work backwards, and it all depends on the dividend yield.
At 3%, you’d need S$32,000 invested, at 4% it drops to S$24,000 and drops further to just S$19,200 at 5%.
Although a
higher yield
means less capital required, it often also means more risk.
Sometimes, these juicy yields are a signal that the business is under some sort of pressure.
Global Dividend Giants That Could Help Pay the Bills
Microsoft Corporation
(NASDAQ: MSFT)
Microsoft makes money from software and computing infrastructure that businesses use every day, from productivity software to cloud computing and, increasingly, AI.
Much of that is recurring, as customers pay monthly or yearly to keep using Microsoft’s products.
During 1QFY2027 (the first quarter of the fiscal year ending 30 June 2027), Microsoft’s revenue rose 19.0% to US$92.3 billion, propelled by a 30.0% gain in Microsoft Cloud revenue and 17% growth in Microsoft 365 Consumer Cloud revenue.
Even as heavy AI spending drove property and equipment investments up 103% YoY to US$39.4 billion during the quarter, Microsoft still generated US$18.6 billion of free cash flow.
Its quarterly payout was also boosted by 8.0% to US$0.98 per share in September 2026.
Although its 0.74% yield looks modest, that consistent payout trajectory is a welcome sign for long-term holders.
Apple Inc.
(NASDAQ: AAPL)
Apple’s iPhones, Macs and iPads pull users into its services, from the App Store to iCloud and Apple Music.
That installed base keeps paying long after the device is bought.
Apple’s revenue rose 11.7% YoY to US$114.5 billion in the fourth quarter of the year ended 26 September 2026 (4QFY2026), with products revenue up 12.5% YoY to US$82.9 billion and services revenue up 9.8% YoY to US$31.6 billion.
Quarterly dividend was up 3.85% YoY, from US$0.26 per share to US$0.27 per share.
Over FY2026, Apple spent US$86 billion buying back shares, against US$11.8 billion on dividends.
So its investment appeal lies more in capital appreciation than income paid out today.
Visa Inc.
(NYSE: V)
Every tap of your card puts a small fee in Visa’s pocket.
As more of the world moves from cash to cards and phones, that network keeps growing.
In FY2026 (fiscal year ended 30 September 2026), Visa’s net revenue rose 15.0% to US$45.9 billion, and returned over US$25.6 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends.
The board has also raised Visa’s quarterly dividend by 16.0% YoY to US$0.78 per share.
A low starting yield of just 0.74% matters less when the payout is growing fast.
These three companies all have
an edge
that rivals find hard to copy and plenty of room to grow globally.
As earnings keep climbing, dividends paid out can also continue to increase.
However, these are just examples of quality dividend payers, and not necessarily the highest yielders out there.
Why Dividend Growth Matters More Than a High Starting Yield
Today’s dividend is just the beginning.
Say your portfolio currently pays US$500 a year and grows 8% annually.
In 10 years, it would be paying around US$1,079, without you adding a single cent!
That matters because subscriptions get pricier too.
With streaming and software providers increasing their prices from time to time, a growing dividend helps you keep pace.
That said, not all high yields mean a good company.
An unusually high yield can also mean that the market expects trouble.
Always remember to check earnings growth, free cash flow, payout ratios and debt before trusting the payout.
How I Would Build a Subscription-Paying Portfolio
Start with a realistic target.
Use the S$960 budget and work out the capital you need using your portfolio’s actual yield, not a convenient 4% or 5%.
This is where mixing helps.
Low-yielding tech names alone would need a much bigger pot to hit S$960 today.
Pairing them with diversified dividend ETFs or other quality income investments can lift your overall yield.
Next, reinvest before you spend.
While you’re building the portfolio, plough dividends back in to buy more shares.
Once your yearly payouts get close to your subscription bill, start redirecting some of them.
Finally, set up a subscription fund.
Park your dividends in a separate cash account and pay your subscriptions from there.
Most global companies pay quarterly, not monthly, so keep a small buffer to smooth out the timing.
What Singapore Investors Should Watch
The big one is
US withholding tax
.
Singapore investors generally lose 30% of dividends from directly held US stocks to the US withholding tax.
That turns a 2% yield into roughly 1.4%, so you’d need about S$68,000 instead of S$48,000 to net S$960 a year.
Currency is another.
US dollar-denominated dividends rise and fall in value when converted to the Singapore dollar, which is what your subscriptions are billed in.
Also, dividends aren’t guaranteed.
Payout ratios, free cash flow and earnings growth tell you whether they can last.
Lastly, don’t overspend to justify investing.
The goal is to build wealth while covering the bills you already have, not to sign up for more because “dividends will pay for it”.
Get Smart: Let Your Investments Pick Up the Tab
Using pocket-change subscriptions as milestones makes passive income feel tangible.
Great compounders like Microsoft, Apple, and Visa can help you get there, but replacing real expenses takes time and steady discipline.
After all, the endgame isn’t just a free Netflix account – it’s letting your portfolio take over your living costs so you depend less on your paycheque.

title: US labour market shows signs of revival with rise in job postings
article:
(Nov 18): A broadening swathe of the US is seeing growth in job openings, suggesting the labour market could break free next year from the low-hire environment that has long frustrated job seekers, according to a new report from Glassdoor and Indeed.

Nearly half of US metro areas had more job postings in late September than a year earlier, the highest share since 2022. That’s up from just one in 10 metros at the start of the year. Postings were above pre-pandemic levels in 299 of 385 metro areas with at least 100,000 residents.

Even so, workers remain generally downbeat about the job market. Employee confidence on Glassdoor fell in roughly 70% of metro areas, including many places where hiring demand has picked up.

“This is a labour market that is very eager to move again,” said Sneha Puri, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab. “It wouldn’t be unrealistic to expect some major movements in the labour market in the next year.”

For early-career job seekers, the figures are still particularly grim. While senior-level postings are up 19.2% since January 2025, entry- and mid-level positions are each down about 4%. That has helped push the unemployment rate among recent graduates up 1.3% since 2023.

See also: US homebuilder sentiment falls to fresh 14-year low on high rates

Even when they do land jobs, many recent graduates are settling for less. Slightly more than half of 2025 graduates were underemployed a year after graduating, up from just under 40% for most of the past decade.

The figures suggest nascent momentum in a job market that has generally been stuck in a low-hire, low-fire mode. Businesses have faced deep uncertainty due to tariffs, changes in immigration policy and higher energy costs. While that’s allowed employees to largely avoid being swept up in mass layoffs, there’s been limited opportunities for those seeking jobs.

title: AI could become pervasive, like the internet, suggests DPM Gan
article:
Deputy prime minister, minister of energy, trade and investment, and chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore Gan Kim Yong, during a fireside chat with Caesar Sengupta, the founder and CEO of start-up Studio C6, on AI, gamely answered questions put to him, including how he personally uses AI.

“I use it to do some analysis. In the past I asked my staff to do research and to put up a paper to understand what's happening around the world, specific issues, trade data, the relationship with different countries. But since I realised my staff used AI to prepare the documents, I decided to use AI too. However you should not take the answers from AI at face value. You have to inject your own assessment, your own judgement, and to see how you can best make use of the information to achieve your objective. So similarly, with this fireside chat, I still have to look at your questions, and the question you asked just now was not in the list of questions,” DPM says.

As DPM Gan views it, like any technological revolution, the outcome of AI on society and business could be quite different from what was expected of it at the start of the revolution. For instance, the internet is so pervasive that we don't think about the internet anymore.

“For us, as the older generation, we came from an analogue world. In time to come, when AI becomes pervasive, AI will become just part of our lives. And for the businesses, they are adopting AI, trying to make use of AI to make their businesses more efficient, more effective, more competitive. That’s the first stage. In time, businesses may use AI as a foundation to build the business,” he says.

Singapore is working to ensure that AI is deployed, developed, and used responsibly. Many Singaporeans are anxious about the impact of AI on jobs, DPM Gan acknowledges. “As Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, we may not be able to protect every job. Some of the jobs will be changed by AI. But we do intend to protect every worker by giving them skills that they're able to take advantage of for new jobs and new opportunities that are created by AI. I'm an optimist. We will arrive on the other side when AI becomes the norm and the rule and to take advantage of AI. I hope in my lifetime I will see the full impact of AI and the benefits it will bring to our people,” DPM Gan says.

title: Copper hits seven-month low as doubts over demand grow
article:
(Nov 18): Copper fell to a seven-month low as a stronger dollar added to downward pressure from doubts over data center demand and gloomy Chinese economic data.

 

Futures dropped 4% on the London Metal Exchange (LME) to as low as US$12,700 a tonne, the lowest intraday level since mid-April. A gauge of the dollar rose ahead of the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting.

A recent selloff in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks has taken some of the shine off copper, which is used in wiring. Worse-than-expected Chinese industrial production and fixed-asset investment figures have also contributed to a broader retreat in metals, with tin down more than 8% at one point and zinc falling as much as 2.8%.

Copper and tin, which are the metals most tied to AI, are posting the steepest declines, said Li Xuezhi, head of research at brokerage Chaos Ternary Futures Co.

Despite strong global growth and manufacturing activity, the usually close relationship between industrial activity measures and underlying demand indicators has broken down, said Nicholas Snowdon, Mercuria Energy Group’s head of metals and mining research, said at an industry conference in Shanghai on Wednesday.

“Copper demand today is closer to a recessionary-like environment than growth environment,” he said. “A lot of the big picture views on copper offer a very positive view of where demand is today — the reality is markedly different.”

Copper fell 3.7% to US$12,733.50 a tonne on the LME as of 9.13am in London. Aluminium dropped 2.2% to US$2,869.50, easing a squeeze cased by a scarcity of LME stockpiles.

See also: Iron ore likely to find a floor near US$80, Chinese analysts say

Stan Druckenmiller, the billionaire founder of the Duquesne Family Office, said on Tuesday at an event in Austin, Texas that he’s bearish on copper. Like many investors, Druckenmiller had been long on the red metal at the beginning of the year.

title: Japanese restaurant chain Skylark eyes more M&A after ramen chain deal
article:
(Nov 18): Skylark Holdings Co, one of Japan’s largest restaurant chains, plans more M&A in 2027, and expects its growth-investment budget to match at least this year’s ¥50 billion, according to company management.

Skylark, which operates around 3,200 restaurants under multiple brands, announced the purchase of ramen noodle restaurant operator Shin-Shin Co for ¥12 billion earlier this month. That follows its acquisition of a Japanese chain specialising in charcoal-grilled fish and set meals called Shinpachi Co earlier this year.

“We’ll continue to pursue M&A,” said chief executive officer Makoto Tani in an interview on Tuesday at the company’s headquarters in Tokyo. The new brands can help the group rejuvenate its existing restaurant network and “be quickly expanded overseas,” he said.

Skylark is forecasting a 17% increase in operating profit to ¥35 billion for 2026, as it grows its restaurant footprint. It is also raising prices to offset higher costs in its home market, where the Bank of Japan increased its policy rate to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September.

The company recently reported a 5.8% increase in same-store sales for the first nine months of 2026.

Skylark is currently formulating its plans for next year, but its investment budget to pursue growth initiatives is likely to be the same as or more than this year’s ¥50 billion, according to chief financial officer Yoshiaki Kita, who also took part in the interview. Around half of that amount was used for acquisitions in 2026, with the rest being used for new store openings, IT and supply chain improvements, he said.

See also: Q&M Dental completes THB 994.5 mil acquisition of 51% stake in Thai dental group

Under Skylark’s medium-term management plan ending next year, it has targeted about three to five acquisitions. It has done four M&A deals since 2024, including a Malaysian purchase.

Skylark already operates about 95 restaurants in Taiwan, its single largest overseas market, but CFO Kita said the company is also interested in building a presence in the US, where it has only two locations.

“The US is a very sophisticated market. Competition in the restaurant industry is also intense. Naturally, we’re going to take on that challenge,” he said, but declined to give a target. “For overseas operations, in particular, we test things such as how to localise the business. Once we determine ‘This works,’ we’ll expand rapidly.”

title: Tencent’s sales miss estimates in setback for founder’s AI push
article:
(Nov 18): Tencent Holdings Ltd’s revenue missed estimates, underscoring the urgency of an effort by China’s most valuable company to reorganise its workforce around a bold bet on artificial intelligence.

The country’s social media leader reported revenue rose 8% to RMB207.3 billion in the September quarter, lower than the average analyst projection. Net income barely grew during the period.

The tepid results raise questions about billionaire co-founder Pony Ma’s efforts to close the gap with long-time rivals Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and ByteDance Ltd in the AI era. Last week, he called on half of Tencent’s 100,000-strong workforce to harness artificial intelligence in search of new growth avenues while urging the rest to try boosting efficiency in its gaming and social media businesses.

Tencent has claimed a spate of early successes in its AI push, releasing an Hy4 model this month that it said ranks among China’s most powerful. Its WorkBuddy office tool claimed 32 million monthly active users in September, more than its direct rivals combined. At the helm of those efforts is Dowson Tong, one of Ma’s key lieutenants, who is driving teams to experiment with products.

However, the company is still playing catch-up with upstarts such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, bringing in former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu to help. Its flagship chatbot has failed to challenge ByteDance’s market-leading Doubao, which started charging subscriptions after cementing its place as the country’s most popular ChatGPT-style platform.

See also: Chinese AI stocks down as US chip curbs hit labs and hyperscalers

Ma slammed Tencent’s AI endeavour as “a leaky ship” in May, then gathered employees at a company anniversary celebration this month where he urged them to contribute more. “If you don’t embrace the ongoing intelligence revolution, you get disrupted. This is a matter of life and death,” Ma said, according to a transcript of his remarks published by Tencent.

Competition in China’s AI arena is only set to intensify with ByteDance preparing to launch a personal AI assistant and Alibaba planning to spin off its chip unit via an IPO in Hong Kong. Complicating matters, Washington this week unveiled new rules aimed at cutting off Chinese access to Southeast Asian data centres, disrupting a vital avenue for training and developing AI.

Much of Tencent’s hopes now rest on WeChat, the ubiquitous app that is already shouldering much of the monetisation burden in areas from advertising to live shopping. WeChat’s native agent, Xiaowei, has been in testing since summer. Executives hope it will morph into an AI-first ecosystem that is central to the everyday lives of more than a billion people.

See also: China’s top AI firms limit cyber capabilities in latest models

Chinese big tech firms have shifted toward building out AI data centres and stocking up on scarce chips even as investors increasingly scrutinise the near-term payoffs of such endeavours.

Tencent’s free cash flow turned negative in the June quarter after it hiked capital spending by 180% to US$8 billion. That is still on the conservative side compared with Silicon Valley giants like Meta Platforms Inc and Microsoft Corp.

Funding a big portion of that spending is Tencent’s mainstay games business. The company has become more cautious about starting projects anew during a global industry downturn while turning to what it calls “evergreen” titles such as Honor of Kings to reap consistent profits.

In global markets, Path of Exile 2 from a New Zealand studio owned by Tencent is scheduled for a full launch in December after an initial rollout two years ago.
